code: d2 <- data.frame(dinfl = diff(yraw$infl), unemp = yraw$unemp[-1]) f2 <- varm(d2, p = 2) round(max(stability(f2)), 3) #> [1] 0.851 ir_lr <- irf(f2, id = id_longrun(), horizon = 300, ci = "none") round(apply(ir_lr$estimate, c(1, 2), sum), 3)    # cumulated long-run matrix: upper-right entry is 0 #>         shock #> response  dinfl unemp #>    dinfl  0.854 0.000 #>    unemp -3.794 3.949 ir_c <- irf(f2, id = id_longrun(), horizon = 40, ci = "wild", nboot = 300, cumulative = dinfl) autoplot(ir_c, responses = dinfl)   # level of inflation after the permanent (first) and the transitory shock set.seed(5) bq_one <- function(rho, n = 200) {   Fm <- (1 - rho) * diag(2); L <- matrix(c(1, 0.5, 0, 1), 2); Pm <- Fm %*% L      # Theta(1) = L, lower triangular   y <- matrix(0, n + 50, 2); for (t in 2:(n + 50)) y[t, ] <- rho * y[t - 1, ] + Pm %*% rnorm(2)   f <- varm(y[-(1:50), ], p = 1)   sum(irf(f, id = id_longrun(), horizon = 150, ci = "none")$estimate[2, 1, ])     # estimated long-run effect } sapply(c(`rho=0.5` = 0.5, `rho=0.9` = 0.9, `rho=0.97` = 0.97), function(r) { x <- replicate(100, bq_one(r)); c(mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x)) }) #>        rho=0.5   rho=0.9  rho=0.97 #> mean 0.5189669 0.4147380 0.4252881 #> sd   0.2146527 0.4264377 0.6305603

code: A <- matrix(c(0.6, 0.2, 0, 0.5), 2, 2); Pc <- t(chol(matrix(c(1, .3, .3, 1), 2))) Ht <- 12 truth <- sapply(0:Ht, function(h) { M <- diag(2); for (i in seq_len(h)) M <- A %*% M; (M %*% Pc[, 1] / Pc[1, 1])[2] }) sim2 <- function(n = 250, burn = 50) {   e <- matrix(rnorm(2 * n), n) %*% t(Pc); Y <- matrix(0, n, 2)   for (t in 2:n) Y[t, ] <- A %*% Y[t - 1, ] + e[t, ]   Y <- Y[-seq_len(burn), ]; colnames(Y) <- c("x", "y"); Y } R <- 100; out <- matrix(0, R, 4, dimnames = list(NULL, c("mse_raw", "mse_smooth", "cov_raw", "cov_smooth"))) for (r in seq_len(R)) {   Y <- sim2()   f <- lp(Y, x, Ht, lags = 2, responses = y); s <- lp_smooth(Y, x, y, Ht, lags = 2)   out[r, ] <- c(mean((f$estimate[, 1] - truth)^2), mean((s$estimate[, 1] - truth)^2),                 mean(truth >= f$bands[, 1, 1] & truth <= f$bands[, 1, 4]),                 mean(truth >= s$bands[, 1, 1] & truth <= s$bands[, 1, 4])) } m <- colMeans(out) round(c(m, mse_ratio = unname(m["mse_smooth"] / m["mse_raw"])), 3) #>    mse_raw mse_smooth    cov_raw cov_smooth  mse_ratio  #>      0.008      0.005      0.872      0.772      0.651

code: set.seed(5); N <- 40; Tn <- 50 ft <- rnorm(Tn); mu <- rnorm(N)                       # common time shock; unit effects d <- expand.grid(t = 1:Tn, id = 1:N) d$s <- 0.5 * mu[d$id] + 0.5 * ft[d$t] + rnorm(nrow(d)) d$y <- 0 for (i in 1:N) {   ix <- which(d$id == i); yy <- 0   for (k in seq_along(ix)) { yy <- 0.7 * yy + 0.5 * d$s[ix[k]] + mu[i] + ft[k] + rnorm(1); d$y[ix[k]] <- yy } } hs <- c(0, 2, 4, 8) res <- sapply(c(none = "none", unit = "unit", time = "time", twoway = "twoway"),               function(f) lp_panel(d, y, s, id, t, horizon = 8, lags = 1, fe = f)$estimate[hs + 1]) round(cbind(res, truth = 0.5 * 0.7^hs), 3) #>       none  unit  time twoway truth #> [1,] 1.007 0.949 0.603  0.529 0.500 #> [2,] 0.841 0.581 0.472  0.271 0.245 #> [3,] 0.515 0.141 0.406  0.127 0.120 #> [4,] 0.403 0.057 0.336  0.020 0.029 pn <- lp_panel(d, y, s, id, t, horizon = 8, lags = 1) pn$nclusters[1] #> [1] 40 round(cbind(estimate = pn$estimate[, 1], se = pn$se[, 1], truth = 0.5 * 0.7^(0:8))[c(1, 3, 5, 9), ], 3) #>   estimate    se truth #> 0    0.529 0.021 0.500 #> 2    0.271 0.036 0.245 #> 4    0.127 0.051 0.120 #> 8    0.020 0.032 0.029 autoplot(pn) +   geom_line(aes(y = truth, linetype = "truth"), data = data.frame(horizon = 0:8, truth = 0.5 * 0.7^(0:8))) +   scale_linetype_manual(values = "dashed", name = NULL) +   labs(title = "Panel LP, two-way fixed effects")

Two estimators: default Newey-West covariance two lags, lag augmentation (one lag plus extra lag, HC covariance). 300 replications; coverage carries Monte Carlo error ±0.02\pm0.02. Pointwise bands cover whole path quarter third replications, one expects 13 correlated 90% intervals. Sup-t bands much better fall short 0.90 target: 0.78 Newey-West 0.84 lag augmentation. code: cover_path <- function(la, lg, R = 300) {   set.seed(42); hit <- matrix(0, R, 2, dimnames = list(NULL, c("pointwise", "sup-t")))   for (r in seq_len(R)) {     Y <- sim2()     bb <- lp_supt(lp_joint(Y, x, Ht, lags = lg, responses = y, lag_augment = la), 0.9, nsim = 2000, seed = r)     hit[r, ] <- c(all(truth >= bb$pw_low & truth <= bb$pw_high), all(truth >= bb$conf.low & truth <= bb$conf.high))   }   colMeans(hit) } round(rbind(`Newey-West (lags = 2)` = cover_path(FALSE, 2), `lag-augmented (lags = 1 + 1)` = cover_path(TRUE, 1)), 2) #>                              pointwise sup-t #> Newey-West (lags = 2)             0.24  0.78 #> lag-augmented (lags = 1 + 1)      0.33  0.84

nb <- m * K; beta <- matrix(0, nb, T)   b <- as.numeric(rbind(diag(0.6, K), c(0.2, 0.1, 0.1))); a <- c(0.3, -0.2, 0.2); hh <- log(c(0.3, 0.2, 0.25)^2)   Y <- matrix(0, T, K); y <- rep(0, K)   for (t in 1:T) {     b <- b + qb * rnorm(nb); a <- a + qa * rnorm(3); hh <- hh + qh * rnorm(K)     A <- diag(K); A[2, 1] <- a[1]; A[3, 1] <- a[2]; A[3, 2] <- a[3]     y <- as.numeric(c(y, 1) %*% matrix(b, m, K) + solve(A, exp(hh / 2) * rnorm(K))); Y[t, ] <- y; beta[, t] <- b   }   colnames(Y) <- c("a", "b", "c"); list(Y = Y, beta = beta) } cover <- function(kq, nrep = 3) {   cv <- numeric(0)   for (r in seq_len(nrep)) {     d <- sim_tvp(); if (max(abs(d$Y)) > 50) next     f <- tvpvar(d$Y, p = 1, ndraw = 600, nburn = 400, nsave_paths = 200, prior = tvp_prior(tau = 40, kQ = kq))     tb <- array(d$beta[, 42:200], dim(f$beta)[1:3]); bq <- apply(f$beta, 1:3, quantile, probs = c(0.05, 0.95))     cv <- c(cv, mean(tb >= bq[1, , , ] & tb <= bq[2, , , ]))   }   mean(cv) } set.seed(5) round(c(`kQ = 0.01 (default)` = cover(0.01), `kQ = 0.05` = cover(0.05)), 2)   # nominal 0.90 #> kQ = 0.01 (default)           kQ = 0.05  #>                0.55                0.76

W=\mathrm{vec}(\hat B)'R'\big[R(\hat\Sigma\otimes(X'X)^{-1})R'\big]^{-1}R\,\mathrm{vec}(\hat B)\ \overset{}{\sim}\ \chi^2(r), \qquad F=W/r\ \approx\ F(r,\,T_e-m).  Variable jjdoes Granger-cause variable kk coefficients pp lags jj equation kk zero (r=pr=p). block-exogeneity test generalises set variables JJ entering set equations GG (r=p|J||G|r=p|J||G|). Granger causality predictive content, structural causation: variable anticipates future (interest rate responds expected inflation) “cause” variable responds . varm dedicated function tests. helper wald_block() defined vignette; exported package. uses fit$B, fit$XtXinv fit$Sigma, takes variable names strings. two F statistics agree exactly single-equation case, confirms Kronecker covariance implemented stated.
code: # H0: variables `from` do not enter equations `to` (all lags). Returns Wald/F statistics. wald_block <- function(fit, from, to = setdiff(fit$varnames, from)) {   K <- fit$K; p <- fit$p; m <- nrow(fit$B); vn <- fit$varnames   idx <- c(outer(sort(match(from, vn)) , (seq_len(p) - 1) * K, "+"))   # rows of B for lags of `from`   cols <- match(to, vn)   sel <- unlist(lapply(cols, function(k) (k - 1) * m + idx))           # positions in vec(B)   V <- kronecker(fit$Sigma, fit$XtXinv)[sel, sel, drop = FALSE]   b <- c(fit$B)[sel]   W <- drop(t(b) %*% solve(V, b)); r <- length(sel)   c(Wald = W, df = r, p_chisq = pchisq(W, r, lower.tail = FALSE),     F = W / r, p_F = pf(W / r, r, nobs(fit) - m, lower.tail = FALSE)) } tab <- t(sapply(vn, function(v) wald_block(fit, from = v, to = setdiff(vn, v)))) round(tab, 4)                                  # row = causing variable; H0: does not help predict the others #>          Wald df p_chisq       F    p_F #> infl  33.8805  4  0.0000  8.4701 0.0000 #> unemp 40.1811  4  0.0000 10.0453 0.0000 #> rate   9.9457  4  0.0414  2.4864 0.0447 round(wald_block(fit, "rate", "infl"), 4)     # a single pair #>    Wald      df p_chisq       F     p_F  #>  4.0282  2.0000  0.1334  2.0141  0.1361 round(wald_block(fit, c("infl", "unemp"), "rate"), 4)  # the rate equation ignores both #>    Wald      df p_chisq       F     p_F  #> 36.4323  4.0000  0.0000  9.1081  0.0000 # cross-check one case against nested lm() fits (F test of the rate lags in the inflation equation) d2 <- as.data.frame(embed(as.matrix(yraw), 3)); names(d2) <- paste0(rep(vn, 3), ".l", rep(0:2, each = 3)) full <- lm(infl.l0 ~ infl.l1 + unemp.l1 + rate.l1 + infl.l2 + unemp.l2 + rate.l2, d2) rest <- update(full, . ~ . - rate.l1 - rate.l2) c(lm_F = anova(rest, full)$F[2], wald_F = unname(wald_block(fit, "rate", "infl")["F"])) #>     lm_F   wald_F  #> 2.014086 2.014086

code: resid_matrix <- function(fit) {   a <- augment(fit)   r <- a[startsWith(names(a), ".resid_")]   r <- as.matrix(r[-seq_len(fit$p), ])   colnames(r) <- sub(".resid_", "", colnames(r), fixed = TRUE)   r } portmanteau <- function(fit, h = 12) {   U <- resid_matrix(fit); Te <- nrow(U); C0i <- solve(crossprod(U) / Te)   Q <- 0   for (j in 1:h) { Cj <- crossprod(U[-(1:j), ], U[1:(Te - j), ]) / Te                    Q <- Q + sum(diag(t(Cj) %*% C0i %*% Cj %*% C0i)) / (Te - j) }   Q <- Te^2 * Q; df <- fit$K^2 * (h - fit$p)   c(Q = Q, df = df, p = pchisq(Q, df, lower.tail = FALSE)) } arch_lm <- function(fit, q = 4) {   U <- resid_matrix(fit)   sapply(colnames(U), function(v) {     e2 <- U[, v]^2; Z <- embed(e2, q + 1)     r2 <- summary(lm(Z[, 1] ~ Z[, -1]))$r.squared; st <- nrow(Z) * r2     c(LM = st, p = pchisq(st, q, lower.tail = FALSE))   }) } jb_test <- function(fit) {   U <- resid_matrix(fit); Te <- nrow(U)   E <- U %*% t(solve(t(chol(fit$Sigma_ml))))          # e_t = P^{-1} u_t with P = chol lower   s <- colMeans(E^3) / colMeans(E^2)^1.5; k <- colMeans(E^4) / colMeans(E^2)^2   jb <- Te * (s^2 / 6 + (k - 3)^2 / 24)   rbind(skew = s, kurt = k, JB = jb, p = pchisq(jb, 2, lower.tail = FALSE)) } fit6 <- varm(y, p = 6) round(rbind(`p=2` = portmanteau(fit, 12), `p=6` = portmanteau(fit6, 12)), 4) #>            Q df      p #> p=2 165.4792 90 0.0000 #> p=6  82.3773 54 0.0077 round(arch_lm(fit), 4) #>       infl  unemp    rate #> LM 29.7822 3.7408 47.5408 #> p   0.0000 0.4422  0.0000 round(jb_test(fit), 3) #>        infl   unemp    rate #> skew  0.271   1.176  -0.405 #> kurt  4.018   7.952  10.400 #> JB   11.808 266.691 491.820 #> p     0.003   0.000   0.000 # residual ACF from augment(): one panel per equation, approximate 95% bounds U <- resid_matrix(fit) acf_tbl <- do.call(rbind, lapply(colnames(U), function(v) {   a <- acf(U[, v], lag.max = 16, plot = FALSE)   data.frame(variable = v, lag = drop(a$lag)[-1], acf = drop(a$acf)[-1]) })) ggplot(acf_tbl, aes(lag, acf)) +   geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +   geom_hline(yintercept = c(-1, 1) * 1.96 / sqrt(nrow(U)), linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +   geom_segment(aes(xend = lag, yend = 0), colour = varm_palette(1), linewidth = 0.8) +   facet_wrap(vars(variable), nrow = 1) +   labs(x = "Lag (quarters)", y = "Residual autocorrelation") +   theme_varm()

VAR(1) ρ=0.9\rho = 0.9 T=200T = 200, 90% bands cover 81% (iid bootstrap), 75% (wild), 88% (Monte Carlo) 89% (bias-corrected iid bootstrap); heteroskedastic errors every method covers 61-75%. proxy-SVAR wild bootstrap cover impact response (13-21% coverage nominal 90% validation/proxy-coverage.R). Use type = "mbb" (default proxy_draws()) varm_proxy_robust(). Sup-t bands lp_supt() -cover: 78% whole-path coverage HAC errors (84% lag-augmented HC errors) nominal 90%. Stochastic-volatility calibration slightly low: 83% coverage volatility--volatility parameter 88% volatility path nominal 90% (simulation-based calibration, 60 replications). TVP-VAR results depend prior (tvp_prior(kQ = )); coverage simulated coefficient paths ranged 56% 79% across two settings. hierarchical sampler mixes slowly: effective sample sizes 70-160 hyperparameters 3000 draws one chain. Use mcmc_diagnostics(). id_zerosign() unweighted: ARRW importance weights implemented, bands partial zero restrictions approximate. missing values, VECM cointegration, panel global VAR, mixed-frequency models, frequentist penalised (lasso) VAR, narrative restrictions. See literature map packages cover . varm_proxy_arw() varm_proxy_gkr() new external replication; 50-replication simulation 90% ARW band covered 91% conventional single-prior GKR band 65% set-identified shock (robust region 91%). title: Compare local-projection and VAR impulse responses — compare_lp_var
text: Economic intuition. Choosing LP VAR bias-variance trade-: VAR extrapolates first \(p\) lags horizons (low variance, bias lag order short long-run dynamics), LP unbiased \(h\) variance growing \(h\). divergence long horizons large relative lp_se signals VAR misspecification (LP noise); agreement supports either. Pitfall: comparison meaningful identical lags ordering, function enforces. VAR responses point estimates (bands).

title: Panel local projections with fixed effects and clustered errors — lp_panel
text: Economic intuition. Panels (countries, states, firms) give identification power: unit effects remove time-invariant heterogeneity time effects remove common shocks, response identified cross-sectional differences exposure \(s\). Clustering unit allows arbitrary serial correlation within unit, essential LP residual MA(\(h\)) process. Pitfalls: fixed effects lagged dependent variables induce Nickell bias \(T\) small (use long panels drop y lags); time effects absorb average response, estimate relative effect; clusters (< 30) cluster-robust bands narrow; heterogeneous responses averaged variance weights.

title: Smooth local projections (Barnichon & Brownlees) — lp_smooth
text: Imposes impulse response smooth function horizon, \(\beta(h) = \sum_{j=1}^J \theta_j B_j(h)\) B-spline basis \(B_j\) (cubic default, equally spaced knots \(0..H\)), estimates horizons jointly penalised least squares: $$\hat\theta = \arg\min_\theta \sum_{h=0}^H\sum_t \Big(\tilde y_{t+h}-\sum_j\theta_jB_j(h)\tilde s_{t,h}\Big)^2 +   \lambda\,\theta'D_r'D_r\theta,$$ tilde denotes residuals horizon-specific regression controls (Frisch-Waugh), \(D_r\) \(r\)-th order difference matrix (P-spline penalty, Eilers & Marx 1996) shrinks \(\beta(h)\) towards polynomial degree \(r-1\) \(\lambda\\infty\). \(\lambda\) chosen K-fold cross-validation contiguous blocks time (preserving serial dependence). Standard errors use HAC sandwich \((+\lambda P)^{-1}\hat\Omega(+\lambda P)^{-1}\), \(\hat\Omega\) Newey-West scores summed horizons \(t\); treat smoothing bias negligible.

title: Smooth local projections (Barnichon & Brownlees) — lp_smooth
text: Economic intuition. Raw LP estimates noisy jagged every horizon estimated ; theory says responses smooth (hump-shaped, monotone decay). Smoothing borrows strength across neighbouring horizons, trading small bias (hump flattened \(\lambda\) large) large variance reduction, LP-vs-VAR bias-variance trade-: smooth LP sits unrestricted LP parametric VAR. Pitfalls: sharp features (e.g. impact jump \(h=0\), sudden reversal) smoothed away; use enough basis functions; bands conditional \(\lambda\), ignoring CV step; one response time.

State-dependent local projections (Auerbach-Gorodnichenko) — lp_state
text: Local projections whose coefficients depend state economy transition function switching variable \(z\). horizon \(h\), $$y_{t+h} = F(z_{t-1})\,[\alpha^L_h + \beta^L_h s_t + \gamma^{L\prime}_h w_t] +   (1-F(z_{t-1}))\,[\alpha^H_h + \beta^H_h s_t + \gamma^{H\prime}_h w_t] + e_{t+h},$$ smooth logistic transition \(F(z) = 1/(1+\exp\{\gamma(\tilde z - c)\})\) standardised variable \(\tilde z=(z-\bar z)/\mathrm{sd}(z)\) (Auerbach & Gorodnichenko 2012, 2013; \(F\to1\) "low" state, e.g. recession \(z\) growth) binary version \(F = 1\{\tilde z_{t-1} < c\}\). state enters lagged one period avoid contemporaneous feedback shock state. \(2\times\) regressors estimated one regression per horizon (C++ engine), Newey-West errors, cross-horizon covariance used test \(H_0:\beta^L_h=\beta^H_h\) pointwise (HAC t-test) jointly across horizons (Wald).

title: Sup-t simultaneous confidence bands for impulse responses — lp_supt
text: Montiel Olea & Plagborg-Moller (2019) sup-t bands. \(\hat\sigma_h\) standard error \(\hat\beta_h\) \(\hat R\) correlation matrix implied joint covariance, band $$\hat\beta_h \pm \hat c_{1-\alpha}\hat\sigma_h,\qquad \hat c_{1-\alpha} = (1-\alpha)\text{-quantile } \max_h |z_h|,\ z\sim N(0,\hat R),$$ computed simulation. band covers entire response path probability \(1-\alpha\) (asymptotically), narrower Bonferroni never narrower pointwise band.

title: Sup-t simultaneous confidence bands for impulse responses — lp_supt

title: Sup-t simultaneous confidence bands for impulse responses — lp_supt
text: Economic intuition. pointwise 90% band statement one horizon time; across 20 horizons chance true path leaves somewhere far 10%. Use sup-t bands want claim whole shape (hump, sign, "response horizon") supported. LP estimates strongly positively correlated across horizons sup-t critical value usually modestly 1.64 (typically 2.0-2.5), 3+ Bonferroni. Pitfall: needs good joint covariance (heavy persistence makes HAC covariances unreliable long horizons) horizons zero variance (normalised impact) ignored.

text: Prior Giannone, Lenza & Primiceri (2015) conjugate Normal-inverse-Wishart BVAR: $$\beta|\Sigma \sim N(b,\Sigma\otimes\Omega),\quad \Sigma\sim IW(\Psi, M+2).$$ prior variance coefficient lag \(l\) variable \(j\) equation \(\) \(\lambda^2/(l^\alpha\psi_j)\,\psi_i\)-scaled \(\Sigma\); constant (nearly) flat. what: Prior for the TVP-VAR (Primiceri training-sample calibration) — tvp_prior
title: Prior for the TVP-VAR (Primiceri training-sample calibration) — tvp_prior
text: Hyperparameters training-sample prior Primiceri (2005). Let \(\hat B,\hat\alpha,\hat\sigma\) OLS estimates first tau observations (lag loss), covariance matrices \(V(\hat B), V(\hat\alpha)\). $$\beta_0\sim N(\hat B,\, c\,V(\hat B)),\quad \alpha_0\sim N(\hat\alpha,\, c\,V(\hat\alpha)),\quad   \log\sigma_{i0}\sim N(\log\hat\sigma_i, 10),$$ $$Q\sim IW(k_Q^2\,\nu_Q\,V(\hat B),\nu_Q),\quad S_i\sim IW(k_S^2\,(1+\dim S_i)\,V(\hat\alpha_i),1+\dim S_i),\quad   W_i\sim IG(1, k_W^2).$$ k multipliers prior standard deviations per-period drift relative OLS standard errors; single influential choice TVP-VAR.

title: Prior for the TVP-VAR (Primiceri training-sample calibration) — tvp_prior
text: Economic intuition pitfalls. kQ encodes fast transmission mechanism (lag coefficients) believed move. kQ = 0.01 prior says coefficient drifts 1% OLS standard error per quarter: 170 quarters standard deviation roughly 13% standard error times \(\sqrt{170}\), substantial gradual change allowed. Raising kQ lets data attribute misfit (outliers, omitted variables, mis-specified lags) coefficient drift, .e. spurious time variation. prior neutral: inverse-Wishart prior whose degrees freedom tied short training sample, posterior Q dominated prior samples typical macro length. Always report results several kQ values compare constant-coefficient fit.

what: Time-varying parameter VAR with stochastic volatility — tvpvar
title: Time-varying parameter VAR with stochastic volatility — tvpvar
text: Bayesian TVP-VAR Cogley & Sargent (2001, 2005) Primiceri (2005), Gibbs-sampler ordering Del Negro & Primiceri (2015): $$y_t = X_t'B_t + u_t,\quad u_t = A_t^{-1}\Lambda_t^{1/2}\varepsilon_t,\quad \varepsilon_t\sim N(0,I_K),$$ $$\beta_t=\mathrm{vec}(B_t)=\beta_{t-1}+\eta_t,\ \eta_t\sim N(0,Q);\quad   \alpha_t=\alpha_{t-1}+\zeta_t,\ \zeta_t\sim N(0,S);\quad   \log\lambda_{}=\log\lambda_{,t-1}+\nu_{},\ \nu_{}\sim N(0,W_i),$$ \(X_t=(1,y_{t-1}',\dots,y_{t-p}')'\), \(A_t\) unit lower triangular free elements \(\alpha_t\), \(\Sigma_t=A_t^{-1}\Lambda_tA_t^{-1\prime}\) \(S\) block diagonal one block per row \(A_t\). Gibbs sweep draws, order, \(\beta^T|^T,\Lambda^T,Q\), \(\alpha^T|\beta^T,\Lambda^T,S\), Kim-Shephard-Chib (Omori et al. 2007, 10-component) mixture indicators \(\log\lambda^T|\beta^T,\alpha^T,W\), finally \(Q,S,W\) (inverse-) Wishart / gamma conditionals. State paths drawn Durbin-Koopman (2002) simulation smoother (cost linear \(T\), quadratic state dimension), C++ R's RNG.

Economic intuition. Time variation \(B_t\) changing transmission mechanism (example monetary policy rule responds strongly inflation Volcker); time variation \(\Lambda_t\) change size shocks (Great Moderation, 2008 2020 episodes); time variation \(A_t\) change contemporaneous propagation shocks. conceptually distinct, model omits stochastic volatility tend push heteroskedasticity coefficients. text: Inference (method). "wild" Mertens & Ravn (2013) / Gertler & Karadi (2015)-style recursive-design wild bootstrap: Rademacher weights multiply residuals proxy jointly. "wild_normal" standard-normal weights (variant studied Jentsch & Lunsford). "mbb" residual-based moving block bootstrap Jentsch & Lunsford: blocks length block drawn jointly residuals proxy, recentred mean corresponding within-block position blocks, VAR re-simulated recursively re-estimated. Block length default Jentsch-Lunsford rule \(\ell = 5.03\,T^{1/4}\) (\(\ell = 20\) \(T = 250\)). Jentsch & Lunsford (2019, 2022) show wild bootstrap asymptotically invalid proxy-SVAR impulse responses, multiplying residuals proxy weight leaves sample covariance \(T^{-1}\sum m_t u_t'\) (almost) fixed, sampling variability impact vector reproduced, moving block bootstrap valid.
